item.title: Students want corporal punishment clause removed from Constitution Bill
item.description: Children should be disciplined with love and guidance rather than physical punishment, with two student leaders calling for the removal of the clause allowing lawful and moderate chastisement from the proposed constitutional amendments. item.content:encoded:
Children should be disciplined with love and guidance rather than physical punishment, with two student leaders calling for the removal of the clause allowing lawful and moderate chastisement from the proposed constitutional amendments.

Year 12 student and Deputy Head Girl of Jai Narayan College, Hefrani Matavou, says Fiji needs responsible parenting and proper guidance rather than corporal punishment.

While making her submission during the Constitution (Amendment) Bill public consultation at World Harvest Centre, Matavou says Section 40 , Subsection 1, Part E , which allows lawful and moderate chastisement for the purpose of correction, should be removed entirely from the draft 2026 Constitution.

Matavou says chastisement involves physical punishment, which cannot be clearly measured as lawful or moderate.

She says the proposed provision contradicts itself because the same section seeks to protect children from abuse, neglect, violence and inhumane treatment while also allowing physical punishment in the name of correction.

Matavou says Fiji should be moving forward in protecting children's rights rather than taking a step backwards by allowing physical punishment.

She says that she can recall her submission to the Constitution Review Commission on this issue. Â

Insert:Matavou on what the children want 23rd Oct 26

She says the Constitution must protect every child's dignity, safety and right to be free from violence, rather than provide a legal basis for the very harm it seeks to prevent.

Matavou says she is still regarded as a child under the law and is making one clear submission: that the entire sentence allowing lawful and moderate chastisement for the purpose of correction be deleted from the draft Constitution.

Meanwhile, 13-year-old Finau Vitukawalu, the Head Girl of William Cross Primary School, has also called for the removal of the same provision, saying children should be taught with love rather than pain.

Vitukawalu says she is concerned that allowing lawful and moderate chastisement could give adults an excuse to hit children and claim it is for their own good.

She says she wants the Constitution to protect children rather than allow any provision that could be used to justify hurting them.

Vitukawalu refers to Fiji's ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1993, highlighting Article 28, Paragraph 2, which states that school discipline must be administered in a manner consistent with a child's human dignity .

S he also refers to Article 19, which requires children to be protected from physical and mental violence, abuse and neglect while in the care of parents or others.

Vitukawalu says children need rules, correction and consequences when they misbehave, but they can learn without being hit.

Insert: VitukawaluÂ on chastisement provisions 23rd Oct 26 Â

Vitukawalu also calls for greater support for teachers and parents, including school counsellors to help children who are struggling or displaying difficult behaviour.

She questions why the behaviour of a small number of students who repeatedly break school rules should be used to justify physical punishment for all children.

The young head girl also calls on churches, the vanua and community elders to help families learn alternative ways of disciplining children.

Vitukawalu expresses concern about children who may be experiencing violent discipline but are unable to speak about what they are going through.

She says children who break rules still deserve protection and should be taught respect by being treated with respect.

Both students are calling on the committee to ensure the Constitution protects children from physical punishment while supporting responsible parenting, effective discipline and guidance.

The final parliamentary vote on the Constitution Amendment Bill will take place on November 2nd, and if it is supported by 66 percent of the Members of Parliament then Fiji will have a national referendum on December 9th.

This is where the registered voters around the country will go to the polls and have the final say on whether they are for or against the Constitution.

The new Constitution will only come into place if majority of the people who vote in the referendum support the document.

item.title: Indian national files report with Fiji Police and Immigration Department regarding alleged recruitment scam
item.description: Authorities are working to verify allegations of a recruitment scam involving an Indian national who claims he lost more than $17,000 in connection with arrangements for travel to Fiji and was later threatened and confined at a residence in Koronivia. Speaking to fijivillage News, the man revealed that he first travelled to Fiji in November 2024 after paying an agent in India approximately $5,800.
item.content:encoded:
Authorities are working to verify allegations of a recruitment scam involving an Indian national who claims he lost more than $17,000 in connection with arrangements for travel to Fiji and was later threatened and confined at a residence in Koronivia.

Speaking to fijivillage News, the man revealed that he first travelled to Fiji in November 2024 after paying an agent in India approximately $5,800.

He claims he was detained by immigration officials upon arrival and returned to India.

He alleges the return tickets had been deliberately arranged and claims the individuals involved had already collected money from the applicants.

He says he contacted the alleged recruiter in December 2024 to find out why they had been refused entry, but did not recover his money.

The man says he met the recruiter again in Mumbai in February 2025, when he was asked to pay a further $1,100 for another permit application.

He alleges that in February this year, he paid a further $10,000 in Mumbai after being promised that a work permit would be secured for him.

He claims he was subsequently issued an invitation letter for a business visa, which referred to sugarcane and farming businesses and identified him as a recruitment officer.

However, he says he had expected to obtain employment relevant to his experience and did not want to recruit other people from India.

The man says he arrived in Fiji on 14th September this year, and went to a residence in Koronivia after receiving a location from the alleged recruiter, and that he stayed at the residence for approximately 36 days.

He claims he was repeatedly asked to make payments in connection with the employment and travel arrangements , and that he made several payments.

He claims he paid US$1,045 through an account belonging to the recruiter's nephew and transferred approximately FJD$2,100 through the alleged recruiter's M-PAiSA account.

The man claims he received no assistance with food or living expenses during his stay in Koronivia and had to pay for his own meals and transportation.

He alleges that he also experienced circumstances that caused him to fear for his safety.

He claims he was locked inside the house and threatened, and was warned against disclosing information about the individual or his activities.

He alleges that he eventually managed to leave the residence on 19th October.

He also says that his business visa expired on 28th September and that he had been given a further 21 days to stay in the country.

He says he had also purchased his own return ticket, costing approximately FJD$2,500, which he claims he was unable to use as planned.

He says the circumstances have left him without secure accommodation and that he has been living in fear while seeking assistance and protection.

The man says he has reported the matter to the Indian High Commission in Fiji and the Fiji Immigration Department.

He is also calling for a wider investigation into what he alleges is a recruitment scheme involving more than 60 people from India and Bangladesh.

He claims some individuals may have paid between FJD$10,000 and FJD$12,000 for applications and related arrangements to work in Fiji , and wants authorities to establish whether others may have been affected by similar promises.

He is urging the Fiji Immigration Department to investigate the alleged recruitment activities and the consultancy permit portal.

The man says he wants his money returned and hopes authorities will investigate the allegations and prevent others from experiencing a similar situation.

He believes he has lost valuable time, career opportunities and the chance to advance professionally after trusting the promises made to him.

Meanwhile, Police have confirmed they are working with relevant authorities to verify his allegations.

Questions have also been sent to the Fiji Immigration Department.
